content: The health sector forums aim to foster collaboration among development partners, elected officials, civil society organizations (CSOs), the private sector, and academic institutions. Recommendations from various assessments, such as the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) reviews, Effective Vaccine Management (EVM) assessments, sector reviews, coverage surveys, Data Quality Self-assessments (DQS), and National Immunization Technical Advisory Group (NITAG) inputs, should be considered to guide planning and decision-making. Step 6 involves analyzing the costs, financing, and funding gaps, as well as mobilizing resources to address these gaps. Step 7 focuses on implementing the comprehensive Multi-Year Plan (cMYP) by obtaining approval, disseminating the plan, executing activities, and monitoring progress. The cMYP should include a detailed analysis of the health sector, strategies for financial sustainability, scenario planning, and the use of indicators for cost-benefit analysis and resource allocation. Developing an annual work plan is essential, which involves integrating and consolidating activities, prioritizing tasks and districts, and establishing timelines, responsible units, and financial resources. The cMYP should be put into action through monitoring and evaluation processes. Consensus-building activities should be developed to engage stakeholders in discussions about cost, financing, and funding gaps. Strategies to reduce these gaps should be identified and revised collaboratively. Indicators and methods for monitoring and supervision should be clearly defined. The WHO-UNICEF guidelines for cMYP for immunization, updated in September 2013, outline a 12-step process. Step 1 involves conducting a situation analysis to identify key content areas, including routine immunization, accelerated disease-control initiatives, immunization system performance, and program strengths and weaknesses. This analysis acknowledges that while the national immunization plan is technically focused, broader health system constraints also impact immunization performance. These factors must be considered when drafting the cMYP and negotiating strategies with stakeholders to address system-wide barriers. Routine immunization programming forms the foundation for achieving cMYP objectives and targets. The situation analysis should review all components of the immunization system, including coverage trends, demand, equity, new vaccine introductions, surveillance, adverse events following immunization, and budget execution. A district-level analysis should identify areas with the lowest coverage, demand, and equity to guide objective and priority setting in subsequent planning steps. Accelerated disease-control initiatives, such as those targeting polio, measles, maternal and neonatal tetanus, hepatitis B, yellow fever, meningitis A, and rotavirus, should be analyzed using performance indicators from previous years. This includes data on routine immunization, surveillance, and supplementary immunization activities. For example, national immunization days (NIDs) and sub-national immunization days (SNIDs) should be evaluated for coverage rates and frequency. Immunization system components should be reviewed based on evaluations and technical assessments conducted during the previous planning cycle. The cMYP should be revised as needed to align with the health sector and planning cycle. National immunization performance indicators should be analyzed annually, with data derived from various sources, including EPI reviews and health system analyses. Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) should be identified to inform the situation analysis and prioritize objectives and strategies. Strengths and weaknesses of the immunization program should be documented, linking them to the previous cMYP and the National Health Sector Plan. Opportunities, such as health-sector reforms or new vaccine introductions, should be leveraged, while internal and external threats, such as health-worker migration or conflicts, should be mitigated. National goals, objectives, and milestones should be developed based on evidence from the situation analysis. These should address challenges such as increasing coverage, reaching underserved populations, introducing new vaccines, renewing the cold chain, and improving budgeting and execution. Objectives should align with global and regional commitments and be consistent with the program's strengths and weaknesses. Strategies should demonstrate how objectives will be achieved and be linked to broader health-sector strategies to create synergies and support resource mobilization. Criteria for prioritizing health interventions include health impacts, strategic value, efficiency, equity, and feasibility. For example, increasing vaccination coverage provides social and economic benefits by reducing preventable morbidity, disability, and mortality. Planning priorities should reflect national health plan values, such as equity, decentralization, and poverty alleviation, to increase the likelihood of securing public resources for implementation. Efficiency should be promoted by minimizing the cost per fully immunized child, while equity should focus on narrowing coverage gaps between different population subgroups. Feasibility should consider institutional and financial capacity for program implementation. The cMYP planning process includes steps to determine appropriate strategies and key activities for each immunization system component. These components include immunization service delivery, program management, human resource management, costing and financing, vaccine logistics, and monitoring and surveillance. For example, immunization service delivery strategies may include implementing the Reaching Every Community approach, while program management objectives may focus on political commitment, policy development, and partnerships with the private sector and civil society. Human resource management objectives may address staff production, placement, and motivation. Costing and financing strategies should focus on resource mobilization, efficiency, and sustainability. Vaccine logistics objectives may include vaccine management, cold-chain systems, and waste management. Monitoring and surveillance strategies should align with global standards for vaccine-preventable disease surveillance and include routine reporting, surveillance of new vaccine introductions, and evaluation of program performance. By following these guidelines, countries can develop comprehensive, evidence-based plans to strengthen immunization programs and achieve national and global health goals.
